title: Media Source Characteristics Regarding Food Fraud Misinformation According to the Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) in China: Comparative Study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional door-to-door HINTS-China survey (Beijing and Hefei, May 2017) that asked respondents yes/no whether they had heard each of 8 food narratives officially identified as rumors and independently confirmed false. It reports the share of respondents who heard at least one food rumor (83.6%), i.e. a self-reported share of people who encountered misinformation, with a stated denominator -> RECALL (exposure). The rest of the paper concerns belief/distrust in those rumors, which is out of scope.

estimates.platform: Survey (self-reported exposure; named channels were interpersonal communication, traditional media, internet portals, social media, public organizations)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who had heard at least one of 8 verified-false food rumors
estimates.denominator: 3,090 adults aged 18+ interviewed door to door in Beijing and Hefei using multistage stratified sampling (2,584 valid questionnaires after list-wise deletion: 1,462 Beijing, 1,122 Hefei)
estimates.definition: Answered 'yes' on a dichotomous item to having heard about at least one of the 8 highly publicized food narratives that were officially identified as rumors before fielding and confirmed false by the study's four-source verification mechanism
estimates.misinfo_def: "Ongoing rumors and fake news regarding food fraud, adulteration, and contamination"; the 8 narratives were "officially identified as rumors" and "It has been confirmed that all of the 8 popular rumors ... are false"
estimates.source_quote: Among the respondents, 83.6% (2584/3090) heard at least one food rumor.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results), p. 1; repeated in Results, p. 6: "An average of 83.6% (n=2584) of Chinese respondents heard at least one food rumor, which included 95.7% (n=1462) from Beijing and 71.8% (n=1122) from Hefei."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is self-reported: each respondent answered a dichotomous yes/no to having heard each narrative. The 8 rumor narratives themselves were selected from 4 government surveillance reports on food rumors and safety incidents and were verified false by an external verification mechanism of four official outlets: People's Daily Online and Xinhuanet, plus Chinese Health Daily News and CNPharm.com, the latter operating under the supervision of the National Health Commission. No inter-rater reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The established measures included a dichotomous answer of yes/no for having heard about each food rumor or incident.
estimates.notes: IMPORTANT ARITHMETIC PROBLEM for the adjudicator. The paper's 83.6% is exactly 2584/3090, and 2,584 is separately described as the number of VALID questionnaires after list-wise deletion ('3090 samples were collected, and the number of valid questionnaires was 2584'), so the headline 'heard at least one food rumor' figure may be a conflation with the valid-response rate. Furthermore the two city figures do not reconcile with it: 95.7% of 1,462 = 1,399 and 71.8% of 1,122 = 806, giving 2,205/2,584 = 85.3%, not 83.6%. I kept 83.6% because it is the value stated verbatim twice (abstract and Results) and R8 forbids substituting a value I computed, but confidence is medium and the estimate should not be treated as precise. Topic coded health_other (food fraud / food safety). ground_truth coded self_report because the numerator is what respondents say they heard; note for the adjudicator that the eight claims were themselves pre-verified false by four external official outlets, so the item stimulus (unlike most recall measures) has an external ground truth.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) City-level recall shares are stated verbatim: 'which included 95.7% (n=1462) from Beijing and 71.8% (n=1122) from Hefei.' Beijing and Hefei are two cities in one country, not separate countries or platforms, so under the one-row-per-country-x-platform-x-measure rule I kept only the pooled figure; an adjudicator who treats the two city samples as separate studies would add these two rows (and should then drop the pooled one to avoid double counting). Note that the two-city comparison is the paper's stated design, which is the argument for splitting. (2) 'The respondents in Beijing were confronted more frequently by food rumors (range 346-1253) than those in Hefei (range 155-946)' is a range of counts with no denominator attached, not a share. (3) The media-channel composition among those exposed ('Interpersonal connection was the most frequent communication source (698/1253, 55.7%), followed by traditional media (325/1253, 25.9%) and internet portals (144/1253, 11.5%)') is the channel mix INSIDE the rumor-exposed group, not a prevalence of misinformation, so no row. (4) Tables 4, 5 and 6 and the K-means low/high 'distrust' clusters report belief in / trust of the specific rumors (e.g. 202/638, 31.7% high distrust of 'counterfeit seaweed'), which the instructions exclude ('Belief in false claims does NOT' count). (5) Table 6 concerns 11 REAL food-safety incidents (facts, 'though 2 of them are not accurate'), so its figures are exposure to true news, not misinformation. (6) '73.6% (out of 2584)' preferring physicians and '36.6% (out of 1462)' / '55.6% (out of 1122)' going online first are information-seeking behaviours, not misinformation exposure.

rob.design: Cross-sectional survey (HINTS-China). Sampling frame: multistage stratified sampling with trained interviewers doing door-to-door interviews of one household member aged 18+ in Beijing (capital, urban) and Hefei (second-tier city, Anhui, rural comparison), 9-24 May 2017; 3,090 samples collected, 2,584 valid after list-wise deletion (1,462 Beijing, 1,122 Hefei). The stated 'response rate was 42.65% for Beijing and 57.35% for Hefei (out of 3090 participants)' cannot be a response rate: the two figures sum to 100% and neither matches 1462/3090 or 1122/3090, so no usable response rate is reported. Instrument: dichotomous yes/no recall for each of 8 pre-verified-false food rumor narratives and 11 real 2016 food-safety incidents, plus a 5-point trust scale, plus 12 media-characteristic and 25 media-source items collapsed into 5 categories. Ground truth: the 8 rumors confirmed false via People's Daily Online, Xinhuanet, Chinese Health Daily News and CNPharm.com. Analysis: descriptives, chi-square, correlation, ANOVA, K-means clustering in SPSS 24. No coder reliability statistics (no content coding). Authors' limitations: reliance on self-report of recall behaviour, no causal claims, and the sample is not a national probability sample and is specific to 2017.
rob.item6_quote: It has been confirmed that all of the 8 popular rumors in Textbox S1 in Multimedia Appendix 1 are false, while the narratives of the 11 food scandals in Textbox S2 in Multimedia Appendix 1 reflect the facts in 2016, though 2 of them are not accurate.
rob.item10_quote: An average of 83.6% (n=2584) of Chinese respondents heard at least one food rumor, which included 95.7% (n=1462) from Beijing and 71.8% (n=1122) from Hefei.
